issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a patient whose index trauma is witnessing domestic violence in childhood, sexual-trauma-specific trigger content is a poor fit unless sexual violence was part of the witnessed events. Nothing else in the profile links the trauma memory or threat meanings to sexual content, so this item is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

Avoiding sex is similarly trauma-content-specific and is not supported by the rest of the trigger, threat, or memory items for witnessed childhood domestic violence. In combination with the sexual-trauma trigger item, it suggests a different trauma theme than the one provided, making the profile clinically incoherent.

vignette:
Samir is a 41-year-old construction worker living alone in a small apartment on the outskirts of a Midwestern city. He is the only son of Middle Eastern immigrant parents, and though he seldom talks about his childhood, the memories that do surface are the ones that have kept him trapped for over three decades. When he was eight years old, he watched his father beat his mother in the kitchen of their home—a scene that lasted no more than a few minutes but that split his life into a before and an after. He remembers certain details with a strange, photographic clarity: the way his mother's earring skittered across the linoleum, the pattern of cracks in the plaster above the stove, the sound of his father's belt buckle hitting the counter. But other parts of that evening are blank—complete holes. He cannot recall who else was home, or how the police arrived, or even what he said when the officers came to the door. When he tries to deliberately retrieve the full sequence, his mind goes empty, as though the memory exists only in isolated snapshots he can never assemble into a coherent story.

In the years since, Samir has learned to live by keeping the world small and predictable. He works construction, a job that demands physical focus and leaves little room for extended conversation, especially about the future. His coworkers have come to see him as reliable but distant—a man who never volunteers for a planning meeting and who walks off site the moment a dispute arises between crew members. He avoids any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, because the moment voices rise, his body reacts before his mind can catch up: his heart pounds, his hands tremble, and he feels a wave of heat that makes him want to flee. He has lost two jobs in the past because he walked off a site after a supervisor raised his voice in frustration—not directed at him, but it didn't matter. The physical reaction came anyway, and he left without explanation.

At work, he spends much of his day watching people. He studies the faces and body language of every foreman, every new crew member, every inspector who walks onto the lot. He looks for the tension in a jaw, the narrowing of eyes, the way a person stands when they are about to lose control. He is certain that if he can detect a threat early enough, he can avoid it. This vigilance extends beyond the job site: when he waits at a traffic light that takes longer than usual to change, he feels a knot tighten in his chest and assumes something bad is happening—a crash, an accident, some hidden emergency that he cannot see but knows is coming. When he sees a police car in his rearview mirror, his hands go slick with sweat, even though he has done nothing wrong. The uniform, the authority, the presence of a person who could intervene or enforce—it all brings him back to that kitchen, though he cannot say exactly why. The officers who arrived that night were kind, but he remembers feeling that their kindness came too late, that they were part of the same world of grown-ups who could not stop what happened in time.

To cope, Samir has developed habits that keep him separate from others. When a conversation veers toward the future—someone asking where he sees himself in five years, or even what he wants for the weekend—he drifts off into a world of his own. He does not do it on purpose; it is as though his mind simply opens a door and steps through into a quiet place where there are no voices, no plans, no uncertainty. He also dwells on how he used to be before the event—the boy he was before he learned to read anger in every face. He imagines that earlier self as carefree, unafraid, though he knows that version of him is gone and can never be recovered. These fantasies and backward glances have become so regular that they interfere with his ability to stay present. His foreman has noticed that Samir often seems to be "somewhere else," and he has been warned twice about not paying attention to safety briefings.

What finally brought Samir to seek help was a series of escalating reactions that he could no longer manage alone. Last month, a police cruiser pulled into the construction site to investigate a minor equipment theft. Samir saw the squad car from across the lot and immediately dropped his tools, walked to his truck, and drove home without telling anyone. He sat in his living room for three hours, shaking. His boss called, furious, and told him not to come back until he could "handle himself." That night, Samir realized that walking away was no longer a solution—it was costing him his livelihood. He is terrified that his life will shrink further, that he will end up alone and jobless, but he is equally afraid that therapy will force him to open the door to those blank spaces in his memory, and he does not know what he will find there. He comes to the first session with his arms crossed, watching the therapist's face for any sign of threat, hoping that maybe this time he can stay in the room long enough to tell the story he has never been able to finish.
